premise.text: The AI Act's concept of minimal risk is not equivalent to low cybersecurity risk
The AI Act does not classify by attack surface, but by direct legal and social impact.
Many minimal-risk systems are publicly accessible, highly scalable, integrated with external data, etc.

Frameworks such as NIST and ENISA show that many systems classified as minimal risk present considerable attack surfaces, which justifies additional security controls even if regulation does not require them.

Unlike the AI Act, the NIST AI RMF does not define a minimal risk category. Risk is assessed based on technical exposure, data flows and attack surfaces, which means that many systems classified as minimal risk under the AI Act still require robust cybersecurity controls.
Systems that are not critical from a legal standpoint can be critical from a security standpoint.
Apply controls proportional to exposure, not to sector.

riskTable.description: Introducing malicious data into training or retraining to alter the model's behaviour.
riskTable.whyMinimalRiskIsExposed: Minimal-risk systems are often trained or fine-tuned with open data, user inputs or continuous retraining. Because they are not considered critical, no strict controls are imposed on data quality and integrity, which allows malicious data to be introduced undetected.

riskTable.description: Manipulating the model through inputs designed to bypass restrictions or change its behaviour.
riskTable.whyMinimalRiskIsExposed: Many minimal-risk systems are interactive (chatbots, etc.). The model accepts direct instructions from the user and there is no clear separation between data and control, which makes it easier for an attacker to manipulate the system's behaviour through text.

riskTable.description: The model executes instructions hidden in external data (documents, websites, emails).
riskTable.whyMinimalRiskIsExposed: These systems are often integrated with external sources (documents, etc.). Because they are not considered high-risk, external content is not filtered or validated as a potential attack vector, allowing hidden instructions that the model executes without distinguishing them from legitimate data.

riskTable.description: Partial or total reconstruction of the model through repeated queries to the API.
riskTable.whyMinimalRiskIsExposed: As non-critical systems, they are often exposed through APIs with weak authentication and without strict limits. This accessibility facilitates attacks using repeated queries to reconstruct the model.

riskTable.description: Inferring whether a specific data point was used in training.
riskTable.whyMinimalRiskIsExposed: Many minimal-risk systems use real user data (text, feedback) to improve performance. Because they are not classified as sensitive, advanced defences are not applied, making it possible to infer whether a specific data point was part of the training set.

riskTable.description: Approximate reconstruction of training data from the model's outputs.
riskTable.whyMinimalRiskIsExposed: In publicly accessible models, detailed outputs make it easier to reconstruct training information, a risk not considered in the minimal-risk category.

gaps.description: This Regulation does not apply to any research, testing or development activity regarding AI systems or AI models prior to their being placed on the market or put into service. Such activities shall be conducted in accordance with applicable Union law. Testing in real world conditions shall not be covered by that exclusion.
gaps.reason:
AI behaviour emerges from training and design choices, regulation that only kicks in at deployment cannot fully influence the factors that cause unsafe outcomes. Without rules governing how models are constructed, developers may choose methods that produce unpredictable or harmful behaviors that later testing can only partially detect.

Regulatory exclusion of development phases institutionalizes uncertainty because it defers risk assessment until deployment, when some core deficiencies may be irreversible or costly to mitigate.
papers: Judge, B., Nitzberg, M., & Russell, S. (2025). When code isn’t law: rethinking regulation for artificial intelligence. Policy and Society, 44(1), 85-97.
Currie, W. L., Leimeister, J. M., Schlagwein, D., & Willcocks, L. (2025). Rethinking technology regulation in the age of AI risks. Journal of Information Technology, 40(3), 236-245.

gaps.description: The AI Act introduces a distinct regulatory regime for general-purpose AI (GPAI) models, imposing primarily transparency, documentation, and information-sharing obligations on their providers. Even where GPAI models are designated as posing systemic risk, the applicable requirements remain less detailed and less prescriptive than those imposed on high-risk AI systems, focusing largely on risk mitigation processes rather than concrete technical safeguards.
gaps.reason:
The AI Act imposes extensive controls and compliance obligations on high-risk AI systems, while establishing comparatively fewer and less prescriptive requirements for other categories of AI, including general-purpose AI models, whether or not they are designated as posing systemic risk.

The AI Act’s overall risk-based structure note that simplified risk hierarchies can distort the reality of AI harms. GPAI models may pose broader or harder-to-capture harms that are not fully addressed by the comparatively limited GPAI obligations under the Act.
papers: Gasiola, G. G. (2025). Rebuilding the pyramid: The AI Act’s risk-based approach using a binary decision diagram. Computer Law & Security Review, 58, 106189.

gaps.description: There are only two provisions regarding cybersecurity which are the following. For high-risk systems art. 15 in which it is stated that "high-risk AI systems must be designed and developed to achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity and perform consistently throughout their lifecycle" (abstract and high level obligations, no indications on how to proceed). Art. 55 (for GPAI with systemic risk) "ensure an adequate level of cybersecurity protection for the general-purpose AI model with systemic risk and the physical infrastructure of the model."
gaps.reason:
There is a lack of attention paid to cibersecurity in the AI Act. There are no cybersecurity provisions for AI systems that are not considered high risk or GPAI with systemic risk.

Complex AI systems like LLMs raise novel and emergent cybersecurity risks (e.g., model poisoning, adversarial attacks) that the legislative text only does not touch on.

The concepts of robustness and cybersecurity in the legal text are imprecise, making it unclear exactly what testable, technical requirements developers must satisfy. There is no clear alignment between legal wording and established machine learning security concepts.

No such cybersecurity obligations apply to providers of other AI systems.
papers: Nolte, Henrik, Miriam Rateike, and Michèle Finck. "Robustness and cybersecurity in the eu artificial intelligence act." Proceedings of the 2025 ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency. 2025.

Novelli, C., Casolari, F., Hacker, P., Spedicato, G., & Floridi, L. (2024). Generative AI in EU law: Liability, privacy, intellectual property, and cybersecurity. Computer Law & Security Review, 55, 106066.

gaps.description: The AI Act, while comprehensive for certain risks, lacks explicit measures addressing some new and emerging AI threats.
gaps.reason: Analysts have observed that the Act provides high-level coverage for traditional concerns (like data privacy or bias), but is “comparatively weak in addressing newer risks like hallucination and prompt injection” attacks.
papers: Jonnala, S., Parida, P. K., & Thomas, N. M. (2025). EU AI Act Underrepresented and Insufficient to Address the Risk and Vulnerabilities of Generative AI. International Journal of Business Analytics (IJBAN), 12(1), 1-27.

gaps.description: Almost no obligations for systems that are not considered high-risk
gaps.reason: The high-risk list focuses on areas like healthcare, employment, education, law enforcement, etc., but omits sectors where AI failures could cause systemic economic or safety consequences. Excluding these domains leaves a regulatory gap for AI systems that could dramatically impact society and security.
papers: Jørgensen, B. N., & Ma, Z. G. (2025). Regulating AI in the Energy Sector: A Scoping Review of EU Laws, Challenges, and Global Perspectives. Energies, 18(9), 2359.

papers.reference: Judge, B., Nitzberg, M., & Russell, S. (2025). When code isn’t law: rethinking regulation for artificial intelligence. Policy and Society, 44(1), 85-97.
papers.abstract: This article examines the challenges of regulating artificial intelligence (AI) systems and proposes an adapted model of regulation suitable for AI's novel features. Unlike past technologies, AI systems built using techniques like deep learning cannot be directly analyzed, specified, or audited against regulations. Their behavior emerges unpredictably from training rather than intentional design. However, the traditional model of delegating oversight to an expert agency, which has succeeded in high-risk sectors like aviation and nuclear power, should not be wholly discarded. Instead, policymakers must contain risks from today's opaque models while supporting research into provably safe AI architectures. Drawing lessons from AI safety literature and past regulatory successes, effective AI governance will likely require consolidated authority, licensing regimes, mandated training data and modeling disclosures, formal verification of system behavior, and the capacity for rapid intervention.

papers.reference: Currie, W. L., Leimeister, J. M., Schlagwein, D., & Willcocks, L. (2025). Rethinking technology regulation in the age of AI risks. Journal of Information Technology, 40(3), 236-245.
papers.abstract: This paper argues that artificial intelligence exposes the shortcomings of traditional regulatory paradigms, challenging Easterbrook’s ‘Law of the Horse’ view that general legal principles suffice. AI’s opacity, autonomy, and systemic risks demand risk-informed, technology-specific governance. We identify the pacing problem, where innovation outstrips regulatory capacity, and propose a tripartite framework distinguishing functional, structural, and relational risks. Comparative analysis of EU, US, UK, and Chinese approaches highlights divergent logics of precaution, market oversight, hybrid flexibility, and state control. Effective governance requires embedding risk into policy design through adaptive, proportionate, and harmonised mechanisms, balancing innovation with accountability. The paper underscores the urgency of global coordination and calls for interdisciplinary IS research to inform anticipatory, participatory, and ethically grounded regulation.

papers.reference: Gasiola, G. G. (2025). Rebuilding the pyramid: The AI Act’s risk-based approach using a binary decision diagram. Computer Law & Security Review, 58, 106189.
papers.abstract: The risk-based approach of the AI Act (AIA) results in a complex normative structure, in which the applicable subset of rules for a specific AI system is determined by the general scope of application and the classification of the system into particular risk levels. A pyramid of risks, a widely accepted explanation of the risk-based approach proposed by the European Commission, fails to provide a comprehensive classification process and does not accurately reflect the risk levels (either directly or indirectly) recognized in the AIA or the relation between classification criteria. This paper proposes a corrective solution to rebuild the pyramid of risks. Given that each AI system must be classified into one risk level and the AIA assigns a specific subset of rules to each risk level, an adaptation of the Commission’s risk levels was necessary.

papers.reference: Nolte, Henrik, Miriam Rateike, and Michèle Finck. "Robustness and cybersecurity in the eu artificial intelligence act." Proceedings of the 2025 ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency. 2025.
papers.abstract: The EU Artificial Intelligence Act (AIA) establishes different legal principles for different types of AI systems. While prior work has sought to clarify some of these principles, little attention has been paid to robustness and cybersecurity. This paper aims to fill this gap. We identify legal challenges and shortcomings in provisions related to robustness and cybersecurity for high-risk AI systems(Art. 15 AIA) and general-purpose AI models (Art. 55 AIA). We show that robustness and cybersecurity demand resilience against performance disruptions. Furthermore, we assess potential challenges in implementing these provisions in light of recent advancements in the machine learning (ML) literature. Our analysis informs efforts to develop harmonized standards, guidelines by the European Commission, as well as benchmarks and measurement methodologies under Art. 15(2) AIA. With this, we seek to bridge the gap between legal terminology and ML research, fostering a better alignment between research and implementation efforts.

papers.reference: Novelli, C., Casolari, F., Hacker, P., Spedicato, G., & Floridi, L. (2024). Generative AI in EU law: Liability, privacy, intellectual property, and cybersecurity. Computer Law & Security Review, 55, 106066.
papers.abstract: The advent of Generative AI, particularly through Large Language Models (LLMs) like ChatGPT and its successors, marks a paradigm shift in the AI landscape. Advanced LLMs exhibit multimodality, handling diverse data formats, thereby broadening their application scope. However, the complexity and emergent autonomy of these models introduce challenges in predictability and legal compliance. This paper delves into the legal and regulatory implications of Generative AI and LLMs in the European Union context, analyzing aspects of liability, privacy, intellectual property, and cybersecurity. It critically examines the adequacy of the existing and proposed EU legislation, including the Artificial Intelligence Act (AIA) draft, in addressing the unique challenges posed by Generative AI in general and LLMs in particular. The paper identifies potential gaps and shortcomings in the legislative framework and proposes recommendations to ensure the safe and compliant deployment of generative models, ensuring they align with the EU's evolving digital landscape and legal standards.

papers.abstract: This paper systematically argues that the AI community should learn from the security community's decades-long experience with transparency. It advocates for explicit threat modeling of AI documentation and disclosure artifacts, arguing that each transparency measure should be evaluated through an adversarial lens — not to reject transparency, but to engineer it with security awareness. It directly supports the concept of treating disclosure artifacts as potential attack vectors requiring assessment.

papers.reference: Hintersdorf, D. & Struppek, L. (2023). "Balancing Transparency and Risk: The Security and Privacy Risks of Open-Source Machine Learning Models." Montreal AI Ethics Institute / Technical University of Darmstadt.
papers.abstract: Argues that publicly available model architecture, weights, and training procedures give adversaries a concrete advantage in mounting attacks (model inversion, membership inference, adversarial examples, backdoor exploitation). Directly supports the idea that technical disclosure about AI systems enables attack vectors that must be assessed.

papers.reference: Vassilev, A., Oprea, A., Fordyce, A., & Anderson, H. (2024). "Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations." NIST AI 100-2e2023.
papers.abstract: NIST's taxonomy of adversarial ML attacks identifies categories where attacker capabilities are directly enhanced by access to technical information about a model. This supports treating each disclosure element as a potential enabler of specific attack classes.

papers.abstract: Identifies information disclosure minimization as a basic defense principle against model extraction and inference attacks, stating that unnecessary information disclosure (e.g., providing confidence scores alongside predictions) directly enables adversarial exploitation.

papers.reference: Schuett, J. (2023). "Risk Management in the Artificial Intelligence Act." European Journal of Risk Regulation, 15(2), 367–385.
papers.abstract: Provides a detailed analysis of Art. 9 AI Act's risk management system obligations. While it does not specifically address disclosure-as-attack-vector, it argues for an expansive, iterative interpretation of Art. 9 that would accommodate incorporating security considerations (including those arising from transparency obligations) into the risk management process.

etsi.establishes:
The standard structures AI security from design to end of life.
It avoids treating security as a one-off activity and enforces consideration of risks during conception, development, deployment, operation and retirement.
etsi.gaps:
Risks are not prioritised by system impact.
High-risk and low-risk systems may apply similar controls.
Under-protection of critical systems enables high-impact attacks.

etsi.establishes:
Requires training on AI-specific security threats.
Training must be regularly updated and role-specific (developers, operators, data custodians).
etsi.gaps:
Training depth is not guaranteed.
Superficial awareness leads to human errors exploitable through misconfiguration or unsafe usage.

etsi.establishes:
Requires analysing functional requirements and security risks before building the system.
Security must be integrated from the start, not added later.
etsi.gaps:
No mandatory technical baseline is defined.
Declarative security without real protection enables early adversarial attacks.

etsi.establishes:
Requires identifying threats, assessing risks and applying proportionate controls.
The process must be reviewed whenever the system or its context changes.
etsi.gaps:
No specific methodology or minimum depth is imposed.
Shallow analyses fail to detect advanced or combined attacks.

etsi.establishes:
Requires systems to allow effective human oversight.
Human supervision may act as a security control where appropriate.
etsi.gaps:
No guarantee that humans can understand or detect complex failures.
Subtle manipulations and systematic errors may go unnoticed.

No requirement for automation or continuous validation.

Forgotten or outdated assets can be exploited or maliciously replaced.

etsi.establishes:
Promotes version control and traceability for audit and rollback.
Enables verification of component authenticity.
etsi.gaps:
Verification is often point-in-time only.
Runtime manipulation enables persistent attacks.

etsi.area: Data and input validation and sanitisation
etsi.establishes:
Requires data and inputs to be checked and cleaned.

Especially relevant during training and retraining phases.
etsi.gaps:
No mandatory techniques are specified.

Sophisticated data poisoning and prompt injection remain feasible.

etsi.area: Protection of confidential data and model weights
etsi.establishes:
Requires proportionate protection of sensitive training data and weights.
Recognises them as critical security assets.
etsi.gaps:
Implicit memorisation is not fully addressed.
Membership inference and sensitive data leakage remain possible.

etsi.establishes:
Requires access controls for APIs, models and pipelines.
Aims to reduce unnecessary exposure.
etsi.gaps:
No minimum policies (rate limits, quotas) are defined.
Model extraction and API abuse attacks are enabled.

etsi.establishes:
Recommends separating development, training and production environments.
Applies the principle of least privilege.
etsi.gaps:
Strong isolation is not mandated.
Privilege escalation and cross-environment leakage remain possible.

etsi.establishes:
Requires AI-specific incident and recovery plans.
Includes restoring known safe states.
etsi.gaps:
Largely reactive.
Adaptive and persistent attacks may remain active for long periods.

etsi.establishes:
Requires a clear vulnerability reporting policy.
Encourages early detection of flaws.
etsi.gaps:
Depends on organisational maturity.
Long-term silent exploitation is possible.

etsi.establishes:
Extends software supply chain security practices to AI.
Requires evaluation of external components.
etsi.gaps:
Insecure components may be justified instead of mitigated.
Backdoors and malicious dependencies can persist.

etsi.establishes:
Requires reassessing models before reuse.
Prevents blind trust in existing models.
etsi.gaps:
No clear technical acceptance criteria.
Compromised models may be propagated.

etsi.establishes:
Requires documentation of data, models, prompts, guardrails, limitations and failure modes.
Supports auditability and maintenance.
etsi.gaps:
Documentation is not automatically verified.
“Paper security” may not reflect real behaviour.

etsi.establishes: Uses hashes to verify authenticity of shared components.
etsi.gaps:
Does not protect during execution.
Runtime model tampering remains possible.

etsi.establishes:
Requires recording data sources (URL, timestamp).
Supports traceability of datasets.
etsi.gaps:
Does not prevent pre-collection contamination.
Pre-existing data poisoning remains viable.

etsi.area: Audit logging of system prompt changes
etsi.establishes: Requires logging changes affecting model behaviour.
etsi.gaps:
Does not cover inference-time manipulation.
Persistent prompt injection remains possible.

etsi.establishes: Requires security testing before deployment.
etsi.gaps:
Continuous red teaming is not mandatory.
Novel post-deployment attacks may go undetected.

etsi.establishes:
Requires logging and behavioural monitoring over time.
Enables anomaly detection.
etsi.gaps:
No metrics or thresholds are defined.
Slow attacks (drift, gradual poisoning) may evade detection.

etsi.establishes: Requires secure deletion of data, models and configurations upon retirement.
etsi.gaps:
External copies and derived models are not fully covered.
Residual information leakage persists.
